In [*Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0) (Nature, June 2024) [[1]](#ref-1), [Sebastian Farquhar](https://sebastianfarquhar.com/), [Jannik Kossen](https://jlko.github.io/), [Lorenz Kuhn](https://lorenzkuhn.github.io/), and [Yarin Gal](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/yarin.gal/website/) (Oxford and Google DeepMind) propose an entropy-based uncertainty estimator for large language models (LLMs) that detects *confabulations* (arbitrary, incorrect generations produced when the model is uncertain) by computing entropy over the *meaning* of sampled answers rather than over token sequences.

> Large language model (LLM) systems, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, can show impressive reasoning and question-answering capabilities but often 'hallucinate' false outputs and unsubstantiated answers. Answering unreliably or without the necessary information prevents adoption in diverse fields, with problems including fabrication of legal precedents or untrue facts in news articles and even posing a risk to human life in medical domains such as radiology. Encouraging truthfulness through supervision or reinforcement has been only partially successful. Researchers need a general method for detecting hallucinations in LLMs that works even with new and unseen questions to which humans might not know the answer. Here we develop new methods grounded in statistics, proposing *entropy-based uncertainty estimators for LLMs to detect a subset of hallucinations — confabulations — which are arbitrary and incorrect generations*. Our method addresses the fact that one idea can be expressed in many ways by *computing uncertainty at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words*. Our method *works across datasets and tasks without a priori knowledge of the task, requires no task-specific data and robustly generalizes to new tasks not seen before*. By *detecting when a prompt is likely to produce a confabulation*, our method helps users understand when they must take extra care with LLMs and opens up new possibilities for using LLMs that are otherwise prevented by their unreliability.

## Method

The method samples multiple answers from the LLM for a given prompt, clusters the samples by bidirectional semantic entailment (two answers are in the same cluster if each entails the other under a natural-language-inference model), then computes Shannon entropy over the resulting meaning-cluster distribution. The clustering step is what makes semantic entropy beat naive token-level entropy. Naive entropy conflates two sources of variation: uncertainty about meaning (the real signal of confabulation) and uncertainty about wording ("Paris" and "It's Paris" carry the same answer but inflate naive entropy as different token sequences). Bidirectional-entailment clustering strips out the wording variation, so the per-prompt scalar correlates more tightly with whether the answer is actually wrong.

In deployment the scalar becomes an abstention signal: threshold it, refuse on high-entropy queries, accept the rest. Because high-entropy queries are disproportionately wrong, refusing them removes more wrong answers than right ones, and accuracy on the retained set climbs. The paper quantifies that improvement two ways. AUROC scores how well the scalar separates right from wrong answers across all prompts (detection quality). AURAC scores how much accuracy actually rises on retained answers as the refusal rate sweeps from 0 to 100% (deployment value). The approach is black-box at inference: it needs sample access but no model internals, no fine-tuning, and no task-specific calibration data. A discrete variant approximates the entailment check with single-forward-pass judgments, trading a small accuracy drop for lower cost.

## Results

Experiments span six LLMs (LLaMA 2 Chat 7B/13B/70B, Falcon 7B/40B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct) across TriviaQA, SQuAD [[4]](#ref-4), [BioASQ](https://bioasq.org/), [NQ Open](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/natural-questions), SVAMP [[5]](#ref-5), and a FactualBio biography-paragraph benchmark the authors construct. Averaged across the 30 task-model combinations on short-answer QA, semantic entropy achieves AUROC 0.790, above naive entropy (0.691), P(True) [[2]](#ref-2) self-evaluation (0.698), and a supervised embedding-regression probe (0.687); performance is stable between 0.78 and 0.81 across model families and scales (Figure 2, the cover image above). The method generalizes out-of-distribution: an embedding probe trained on one task drops sharply on another, while semantic entropy maintains near-training performance. Applied to FactualBio, semantic entropy over atomic sub-claims flags unsupported biographical facts and outperforms the paragraph-adapted P(True) baseline, supporting the claim that the signal transfers from short-answer QA to long-form generation.

## My Notes

- **Entailment clustering is the critical step, and the paper does stress-test it.** The meaning-cluster assignment uses a natural-language-inference (NLI) model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI [[6]](#ref-6), or the generator LLM itself in an LLM-as-judge variant). The paper's ablations show results are stable across NLI backbones and stable when generator and judge share a model, which addresses the obvious circularity worry. The remaining open question is scope-specific: on legal, medical, or evaluative judgments, frontier LLMs disagree about meaning among themselves, so entailment clustering cannot be presumed to converge to ground-truth equivalence. [Conformal factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) [[3]](#ref-3) relies on a related claim-decomposition premise and hits the same boundary condition.
- **The OOD-generalization result carries the paper.** Hallucination-detection methods that depend on in-distribution examples (P(True) [[2]](#ref-2)'s few-shot priors, and supervised embedding regression) degrade sharply when the test task differs from the calibration task. Semantic entropy needs no calibration set and transfers across the six datasets without loss, which matters because real-world deployment distributions are never exactly the ones used to train a detector. This is a cleaner version of the argument [Kadavath et al.](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/) made for self-evaluation, without the extra cost of a second forward pass per sample.
- **Composability with fact-verification pipelines is the natural next step.** Semantic entropy flags *which* generations to distrust; benchmarks like AVeriTeC [[7]](#ref-7) and HoVer [[8]](#ref-8) tell you *why* (what evidence does or doesn't support the claim), and tools like [FLEEK](/posts/20231102-fleek-fact-verification/) retrieve evidence from knowledge graphs and the web to make that verdict concrete. A pipeline that routes high-semantic-entropy generations into explicit claim-verification against retrieved evidence would give a user both the uncertainty flag and the remediation path. The paper notes this direction in the discussion but doesn't test it.
- **Part of the "sample $N$, then aggregate" family, with a structural limit they all share.** Semantic entropy shares the same inference backbone as self-consistency [[9]](#ref-9), [CLM](/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/), and [SelfReflect](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/): $N$ forward passes per query at temperature > 0. What differs is what each method does with the sample pool.
  - Self-consistency majority-votes to pick a single answer.
  - CLM applies a conformal stopping rule and returns a calibrated candidate set.
  - Semantic entropy clusters by meaning and emits a scalar abstention signal.
  - SelfReflect (same Oxford + DeepMind lab) summarizes the internal distribution and scores the summary's fidelity to the samples.

  Semantic entropy is closest to SelfReflect by output type (per-query scalar) and to [conformal factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) by goal (hallucination mitigation at deployment, black-box at inference). All four pay the same $N\times$ inference cost, and the choice among them is about which signal the downstream system needs.

  The shared structural limit: the signal is *sample diversity*, not factuality. If a model confabulates consistently (its training distribution pins it to the same wrong answer across sampling temperatures), all samples cluster together, semantic entropy is low, and the method signals "confident" when the answer is in fact wrong. The AUROC gains hold for the subset of hallucinations that produce inter-sample disagreement (the confabulation scope the paper is careful to name) but do not extend to the systematic-bias case.
